title: Blood group, antibodies and anti-D
blurb: Use blood group and antibody results to protect RhD-negative women and their babies: routine prophylaxis, sensitising events and care after birth.
question: Zofia is RhD-negative with no antibodies at booking. At 22 weeks she falls on her front and has some vaginal bleeding. She had no anti-D earlier in the pregnancy. What should the midwife arrange, within what time frame, and does this change her routine 28-week care?

teach.h: Why blood group matters in pregnancy
teach.body: Formally: haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) occurs when maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells; the commonest serious cause is anti-D, formed when an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal blood. In plain English: if a woman's blood is 'D negative' and her baby's is 'D positive', a small leak of the baby's blood can teach her immune system to attack this or a future baby. Anti-D immunoglobulin, given in time, prevents her making those antibodies.
teach.cite: NHS HDFN page (reviewed March 2026); BCSH anti-D guideline (Transfusion Medicine 2014)

teach.caption: Anti-D prophylaxis does not work once a woman has made her own (immune) anti-D; she needs extra monitoring instead.

items.label: Blood group, RhD status, antibody screen
Offer fetal RHD genotyping
items.sub: from her own blood: baby D negative means no anti-D needed

items.label: FBC, group and antibodies, THEN RAADP
items.sub: take the sample before the first routine dose

items.label: Cord blood group
items.sub: baby D positive: anti-D within 72 hours

teach.caption: NICE NG201 1.2.16 and TA156 (RAADP); BCSH 2014 anti-D guideline.

teach.body: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (RAADP) is offered to every RhD-negative woman who is not already sensitised, around 28 weeks (one or two doses, by local regimen). Anti-D for a sensitising event is given as soon as possible and within 72 hours of that event (some protection up to 10 days if the deadline is missed). They are separate: RAADP still goes ahead after event anti-D, and event anti-D is still given after RAADP.

children.label: No anti-D for miscarriage, threatened miscarriage, ectopic or abortion

teach.caption: NICE NG201 1.4.16: offer anti-D for vaginal bleeding after 13 weeks if RhD-negative and at risk of isoimmunisation; also refer to secondary care (1.4.17).

teach.body: Zofia has had two sensitising events (abdominal trauma and bleeding) after 20 weeks. The midwife refers her for same-day obstetric review, takes a blood sample for a fetomaternal haemorrhage (FMH) test, and arranges anti-D as soon as possible, within 72 hours. At 28 weeks, Zofia still has her FBC, group and antibody sample taken first and is still offered RAADP: the earlier anti-D does not replace it.

teach.text: Two classic errors: skipping RAADP because 'she already had anti-D this pregnancy', and giving RAADP before taking the 28-week antibody sample (the injected anti-D would then show up in the screen).

items: Take cord blood for the baby's ABO and RhD group.
Baby RhD-positive and mother not sensitised: offer anti-D within 72 hours of birth.
Test the mother's blood for FMH; extra doses if the bleed is larger than the standard dose covers.
Intrauterine death with no baby sample: give anti-D within 72 hours of diagnosis.
Keep auditable records of every anti-D issue and administration.
Booking: blood group, RhD status and antibody screen; RhD-negative women can be offered fetal RHD genotyping.
28 weeks: FBC, group and antibodies taken BEFORE RAADP.
RAADP for RhD-negative women who are not sensitised; dosing follows the local regimen.
Sensitising event: anti-D as soon as possible, within 72 hours; FMH test after 20 weeks.
RAADP and event anti-D are separate: one never cancels the other.
Already sensitised (immune anti-D): prophylaxis will not work; extra scans and monitoring instead.

summary: You can now explain how RhD sensitisation happens and plan blood group care at booking, 28 weeks and after birth. You can also recognise sensitising events and give anti-D within 72 hours, alongside and separate from routine prophylaxis.

A.q: Lena is RhD-negative and not sensitised. At her 28-week appointment, in what order should the midwife carry out her care?
options: Give RAADP first, then take the group and antibody sample
Take the group and antibody sample, then give RAADP
Give RAADP and send no further blood sample at 28 weeks
Take the sample, then give RAADP once the result is back
A.why: The 28-week blood group and antibody screen must be taken before the first routine anti-D injection (BCSH 2014; NG201 1.2.16).

whyNot.0: Anti-D given first would be detected in the antibody screen and confuse the result.
whyNot.2: NG201 includes a 28-week FBC, group and antibody test.
whyNot.3: RAADP is not delayed for the result; the sample has to be taken first.

A.q: Within what time of a potentially sensitising event should anti-D be given to an RhD-negative, non-sensitised woman?
options: Within 24 hours of the event
Within 7 days of the event
At her next routine antenatal appointment
As soon as possible, within 72 hours
A.why: Anti-D should be given as soon as possible and within 72 hours; if missed, some protection may be offered up to 10 days (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: 24 hours is stricter than the guideline; the standard window is 72 hours.
whyNot.1: Seven days is beyond the 72-hour standard; 10 days is a late fallback, not the target.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a routine visit risks missing the 72-hour window.

A.q: Which woman needs anti-D prophylaxis after an event, assuming each is RhD-negative and not sensitised?
options: Femi, 30 weeks, after a fall onto her abdomen
Nell, 9 weeks, with light painless spotting
Ada, 26 weeks, after a normal glucose test
Joy, 15 weeks, after a routine booking scan
A.why: Abdominal trauma is a potentially sensitising event (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.1: Anti-D is not offered for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks (NICE NG126 1.18.1).
whyNot.2: A glucose tolerance test involves no fetomaternal bleeding.
whyNot.3: A routine ultrasound scan is not a sensitising event.

B.q: Rosa, RhD-negative, had anti-D at 18 weeks after an amniocentesis. She is now 28 weeks and her antibody screen is negative. What should the midwife offer?
options: No RAADP, as she was covered at 18 weeks
A Kleihauer test before deciding on RAADP
RAADP as usual, as it is a separate entity
RAADP after the 34-week appointment
B.why: RAADP is a separate entity, given regardless of and in addition to any anti-D given for a sensitising event (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: Earlier event anti-D does not replace routine prophylaxis.
whyNot.1: An FMH test is for events after 20 weeks, not a gate for RAADP.
whyNot.3: Delaying RAADP leaves her unprotected through the third trimester.

B.q: Bea is RhD-negative and not sensitised. Her baby's cord blood is RhD-positive. What should be offered?
options: Anti-D within 72 hours, with an FMH test
Anti-D at her 6-week GP check
No anti-D as RAADP covered the birth
Anti-D within 72 hours, no tests needed
B.why: If the baby is RhD-positive, a non-sensitised RhD-negative woman should be offered anti-D within 72 hours of birth, with an FMH test to decide whether more is needed (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.1: Six weeks is far beyond the 72-hour window.
whyNot.2: Birth is a sensitising event; RAADP does not cover it.
whyNot.3: An FMH test is needed to check whether the standard dose is enough.

B.q: Meera's antibody screen at booking shows immune anti-D from a previous pregnancy. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Routine RAADP at 28 weeks
Anti-D after any bleeding episode
Postnatal anti-D within 72 hours
Specialist monitoring for HDFN
B.why: Once a woman has her own immune anti-D, prophylaxis will not work; she is offered extra scans and blood tests to monitor the baby (NHS HDFN page).

whyNot.0: RAADP is for women who are not already sensitised.
whyNot.1: Prophylactic anti-D cannot prevent sensitisation that has already happened.
whyNot.2: Postnatal prophylaxis is for non-sensitised women.

C.q: Tara, 24 weeks, RhD-negative and not sensitised, attends with unexplained fresh vaginal bleeding. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Reassure her and review the bleeding at her next visit
Anti-D within 72 h, FMH test, secondary care review
Anti-D at 28 weeks alongside her routine RAADP dose
An FMH test first, then anti-D if the result is positive
C.why: Bleeding after 13 weeks needs secondary care review (NG201 1.4.17) and anti-D (1.4.16); after 20 weeks give anti-D within 72 hours with an FMH test (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: Unexplained bleeding after 13 weeks needs referral and anti-D now.
whyNot.2: Waiting until 28 weeks misses the 72-hour window.
whyNot.3: Anti-D is given for the event; the FMH test decides whether extra anti-D is needed.

C.q: Una is RhD-negative. Fetal RHD genotyping from her blood shows her baby is RhD-negative. What does this mean for her care?
options: She still needs RAADP at 28 weeks
She needs anti-D after any bleeding
Anti-D prophylaxis is not needed
She needs a cord sample before anti-D
C.why: If the baby's predicted blood type is D negative there is no risk of HDFN from anti-D, so anti-D prophylaxis is not offered (NHS HDFN page; NG201 1.2.16 with NICE fetal RHD genotyping guidance).

whyNot.0: RAADP protects against an RhD-positive baby; this baby is RhD-negative.
whyNot.1: Event anti-D is aimed at RhD-positive fetal cells, which are not present.
whyNot.3: Anti-D is not indicated, so there is no anti-D decision to wait for.

C.q: Kemi, RhD-negative and not sensitised, has a confirmed intrauterine death at 33 weeks. Birth is planned in 2 days. When should anti-D be given?
options: Within 72 hours of the diagnosis
Within 72 hours of the birth
After the cord blood group result
At the postnatal follow-up visit
C.why: With an intrauterine death, anti-D should be given within 72 hours of the diagnosis, irrespective of the time of birth (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.1: Timing runs from the diagnosis, not the later birth.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a cord sample may miss the window and may not be possible.
whyNot.3: This is well beyond the 72-hour window.

reteach.title: A lock and two keys
reteach.question: Picture the woman's immune system as a lock that anti-D keeps closed. When is the lock checked, and which 'key' keeps it shut?

blocks.body: Check: blood group and antibodies at booking and 28 weeks. Protect: routine anti-D (RAADP) at about 28 weeks for every non-sensitised RhD-negative woman. React: extra anti-D within 72 hours of any sensitising event and after the birth of an RhD-positive baby. Protect and react are two separate keys, and both may be needed.

blocks.text: Sample first, then RAADP. And an earlier dose for a bleed does not cancel routine prophylaxis.

explain.body: Blood group, RhD status and antibody screen at booking. At 28 weeks, offer FBC, blood group and antibodies, taking the sample before the first RAADP injection.

test.q: Why is the 28-week antibody sample taken before giving RAADP?
options: The injection works less well if it is given first
So the screen does not detect the injected anti-D
The sample result decides which RAADP regimen to use
Anti-D given first makes the blood sample clot
test.why: The 28-week sample is the second antibody screen of pregnancy; taking it after RAADP would detect the injected (passive) anti-D (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: The order does not change how well anti-D works.
whyNot.2: The screen checks for antibodies, not product choice.
whyNot.3: Anti-D does not cause the sample to clot.

explain.body: Any event that may let fetal blood enter the mother's circulation: invasive procedures, bleeding, ECV, abdominal trauma, pregnancy loss, intrauterine death and birth.

test.q: Which of these is a potentially sensitising event in an RhD-negative woman at 37 weeks?
options: A membrane sweep consultation
External cephalic version
A routine fundal height check
A urine dipstick test
test.why: External cephalic version is listed as a potentially sensitising event (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: A discussion about a sweep involves no fetomaternal bleeding.
whyNot.2: Measuring fundal height is not a sensitising event.
whyNot.3: A urine test cannot cause fetomaternal haemorrhage.

explain.body: Give anti-D as soon as possible, within 72 hours of the event. Between 12 and 20 weeks no FMH test is needed; after 20 weeks an FMH test (for example Kleihauer) decides whether more anti-D is needed.

test.q: An RhD-negative, non-sensitised woman at 16 weeks has a threatened miscarriage with bleeding. What is required?
options: An FMH test before any anti-D is given
No anti-D until she reaches 20 weeks
Anti-D within 72 hours, no FMH test
Anti-D at 28 weeks together with RAADP
test.why: For events between 12 and 20 weeks, give anti-D within 72 hours; an FMH test is not required (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.0: An FMH test is not required before 20 weeks.
whyNot.1: Anti-D is indicated now for a sensitising event after 12 weeks.
whyNot.3: Waiting until 28 weeks misses the 72-hour window.

explain.body: Cord blood is grouped. If the baby is RhD-positive, offer the non-sensitised RhD-negative mother anti-D within 72 hours and test her blood for FMH to see if extra anti-D is needed.

test.q: After birth, what decides whether a non-sensitised RhD-negative woman is offered anti-D?
options: The baby's RhD group from cord blood
Whether she had RAADP antenatally
The mode of birth she had
Her haemoglobin on day 1
test.why: Cord blood ABO and RhD typing is performed; if the baby is RhD-positive, anti-D is offered within 72 hours (BCSH 2014).

whyNot.1: RAADP does not cover the birth; the baby's group decides.
whyNot.2: Vaginal, instrumental and caesarean births are all sensitising events.
whyNot.3: Haemoglobin does not determine the need for anti-D.
